headline: Hidden State, Cancelled Signals, and Borrowed Behavior: Notes on Eight Recent Items
narrative_html:
Hidden State, Cancelled Signals, and Borrowed Behavior: Notes on Eight Recent Items

A recurring problem in these items is that something important is missing from the place where a decision is made, and cleverness in the decision-maker cannot supply it. A team of agents lacks a shared record of what changed. A training filter averages away the very drift it is meant to catch. A learned irrigation planner cannot be trusted to write its own physical laws. A city with no trajectory data cannot be modeled by a system that memorized another city's street names. Even the biology of aging is being re-described as the erosion of a boundary that once held cells in place. The items differ widely in field and in how solid they are, and they are worth taking one at a time.

When every agent is right and the team is still wrong

This paper names a failure that anyone who has run multi-agent LLM workflows will recognize: each agent makes a sensible move given what it can see, yet the combined result is invalid. The authors call it a global coherence problem and argue that it is a failure of shared state, not of model intelligence. Their formal core is an Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem. If several different worlds produce the same observation, a policy can guarantee a valid action only when those worlds share at least one admissible action. If k indistinguishable worlds demand pairwise-disjoint actions, the best any randomized policy can do in the worst case is 1/k. Extra reasoning, roles, messages or samples cannot help, because the missing information was never in the context.

The theorem is essentially a pigeonhole argument, and I would not call it deep mathematics. Its value is in the engineering claim it justifies: stop asking models to reconstruct hidden facts and have a harness own the authoritative state and gate commits. The authors package this as a runtime semantics built from topology, category, groupoid and sheaf structures, plus a minimal history that keeps only distinctions that change legal futures. The sheaf language is the idea that local views must glue into one consistent world. The abstract does not show whether that machinery does real work or mostly dresses up a simple design principle.

The empirical results are striking but small. On a controlled revision benchmark, a frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible and 12–17/40 when it is hidden, which is consistent with the 1/3 chance level. Restoring one authoritative fact brings it back to 40/40. On TeamBench, ordinary teams broke a shared budget in 5 of 5 runs, a visible live count still left 4 of 5 violations, and enforcement at commit time left none. In tau2-bench Telecom, checking only current state scored 0.07 after silent reverts, against 1.00 for the harness. The authors also report that a conventional solver ties the harness when it already owns the complete state, which fits their own prediction and is an honest limit. With five runs per condition and designed benchmarks, I read this as a clean demonstration of the mechanism, not evidence about how often real deployments hit it. The practical advice, though, is sound: put invariants such as budgets and ordering where they are enforced at commit time, not where they are merely visible to the model.

What it takes to formally prove a tiny automaton

This is a tutorial post by a programmer who worked a textbook problem in Lean and wrote up the experience for software engineers. The problem is Sipser's exercise 1.32. The alphabet consists of columns of three bits, so a string encodes three binary numbers stacked as rows. The language B contains the strings where the bottom row equals the sum of the top two. The task is to show B is regular, which means building a finite automaton with fixed memory that recognizes it.

The insight is the one anyone who learned column addition would reach. The only thing carried between columns is the carry bit. But numbers are written most significant bit first, so a left-to-right machine would face the carry in the wrong direction. The fix is to build a DFA for the reversal of B, which sees the least significant column first and tracks the carry. Regular languages are closed under reversal, so B is regular as well. The informal proof is a few lines.

The post's real subject is how much more it takes to formalize those lines. From the table of contents, the Lean work involves a specification and an implementation, then a run invariant proved by induction, with a base case and an inductive step. It also involves splitting a run into its first step and the rest, and arguing about how the least significant bit contributes to the sum. Mathlib supplies the closure theorem, which is why the author chose Lean. The extract cuts off before the Lean code, so I cannot judge the proof's size or style. The analogy to program verification is the useful part: the specification states what should hold, the implementation is a machine, and the invariant is the bridge that makes the induction go through. It is an accessible and honest illustration of why verification is laborious even for trivial systems, but it is teaching material, not new research.

Mimir: letting an LLM propose but never touch the physics

Mimir targets a regime where LLM agents are rarely evaluated: long-running physical control, where actions change future states and errors compound over a whole growing season. The domain is irrigation, with daily decisions interacting with soil-water dynamics. The design separates two timescales. Quickly, the LLM's output goes through a structured physical interface and a deterministic simulator, producing a proposal that is numerically checked, revised, and then passed through bounded deterministic action selection before anything is executed. Slowly, recurring failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles that condition later proposals, while the physical model, the evaluator and the execution constraints stay immutable.

The central idea is a division of authority: the language model supplies semantic reasoning and the numerical machinery keeps physical truth and actuator control. That is a sensible template for any safety-relevant setting, and the principle that an agent may learn heuristics but not rewrite its own safety rules is the most transferable piece.

The reported results are that Mimir has the lowest aggregate control cost among the evaluated references across multiple sites, crops and years, and uses about 51% less irrigation than a replay of the historical schedule. Ablations that remove forward simulation, verified revision or persistent context all raise cost, and larger models do not give monotonic gains. The last point is interesting, since it suggests the scaffolding matters more than raw model size. The caveats are what the abstract leaves open. The evaluation is retrospective, so there was no field deployment. I cannot tell how the cost function weighs water against yield stress. Nor can I tell how independent the evaluator is from the simulator the agent consults. Halving water use against a historical schedule is also a comparison against a baseline that may not have been tuned for water saving.

FLUX 3 Image: a product page, not a paper

The extract is a marketing page, and much of it is padded with invisible characters. It lists capabilities and gives almost no measurements, so the claims here are the vendor's and I could not check them. The headline feature is layout control. You can supply bounding boxes with element IDs and descriptions, and the example includes a title in a thin cream serif, a pale concrete dome, silhouetted swimmers and a seated crowd, each with coordinates that look normalized to a 0–1000 range. The page also says you can skip the boxes and just write a prompt, and that the model has strong prompt following and a native grasp of composition.

Other claimed features are multi-edit operations that change several things without touching the rest of the image, such as recoloring a wetsuit and board box by box. It also mentions combining up to ten reference images into one composition, generation at native 2K and 4K (the sample is a 5456 × 3072 soba shop), and "pixel perfect" editing that preserves everything outside the edit region. A closing line says it is "designed for agents," which presumably means a structured, programmable interface.

Spatial grounding and localized editing are real pain points in image generation, so the feature list targets the right problems. But the extract has no benchmarks, failure cases, pricing or architecture detail. Whether edits are truly pixel-identical, or how well the box-driven layout holds up with crowded scenes, is something only independent testing can show.

CARM: stopping drift from cancelling itself out

In reinforcement learning for LLMs, the model that generates rollouts and the model being trained are often slightly out of sync, because the policy has been updated since sampling or the two engines differ numerically. This makes sampled responses off-policy. One common remedy is sequence-level masking, which drops an entire response from the gradient if it looks too stale. A popular test uses the length-normalized geometric mean of the per-token probability ratios, which is the exponential of the average log-ratio.

The authors point out a flaw. Log-ratios are signed, so a response in which some tokens became much more likely and others much less likely can average out to roughly zero and pass the test, even though the policy has moved substantially. CARM fixes this by taking the absolute value of each token's log-ratio before averaging. The paper proves that an accepted response satisfies a joint bound on the fraction of tokens whose ratio is outside a prescribed band and on their mean log-distance beyond the band's edge.

Reported gains are up to 3.13 percentage points in mean@16 averaged across AIME 2024, 2025, 2026 and BeyondAIME versus geometric-mean masking, and 2.88 points in average pass@1 over the strongest baseline on four code benchmarks. This is a small, principled change, and the cancellation argument is persuasive. The likely cost is that stricter masking discards more samples, and the abstract says nothing about this or the model sizes involved. Note too that "up to" 3.13 points means the typical gain may be smaller. I would treat it as a sensible refinement, not a breakthrough.

Aging as the erosion of cell identity

This is a newsletter piece (Eric Topol's Ground Truths) summarizing two papers: one in Nature from Vadim Gladyshev's group at Harvard, and one in Cell from Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte's team at Altos Labs. They are said to complement the wear-and-tear picture of aging with a loss-of-identity model. The author says explicitly that the relative contribution of the two is unknown.

The model runs as follows. A cell's identity is maintained by a three-layer regulatory grammar. A fast layer, with transcription factors such as AP-1, responds in minutes to hours. An intermediate layer handles state transitions over days to weeks. A slow layer, based on chromatin architecture, is the hard boundary that locks identity in. In Waddington's old landscape metaphor, a differentiated cell sits in a deep valley. With age the valleys flatten and the basins get shallow, which is called decanalization. The polycomb complex PRC2 is cast as the sculptor of that landscape, and the summary says epigenetic clocks, which predict lifespan across 348 mammalian species, are in effect measuring the pace of PRC2-related erosion. Chronic inflammation is said to override the fast layer and block PRC2, and some chromatin changes persist after inflammation resolves.

The Cell paper contributes the idea of mesenchymal drift, in which cells shift toward a fibroblast-like state, laying down extracellular matrix and scar in a self-reinforcing loop. It was reportedly verified in 46 tissue types and linked to conditions from atherosclerosis to macular degeneration and Alzheimer's disease. Proposed interventions are caloric restriction, brief partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors (including OSK without c-Myc, in a pilot for optic nerve damage), and lithium acting on GSK3β. The framing is coherent and testable, but this is a secondary account whose extract ends mid-sentence. The link between lithium orotate and Alzheimer's is explicitly speculative, and caloric restriction results in primates are noted as inconsistent. A claim that loss of identity is both driver and result of aging is also hard to disentangle from correlation, so I would hold it as a promising hypothesis.

SPHERE: VR scene generation that remembers your taste

SPHERE addresses a practical irritation in LLM-driven 3D indoor scene generation for virtual reality: the system forgets your preferences between sessions, so you repeat the same physically tiring corrections with controllers. The framework extracts persistent spatial preferences from speech and controller edits. Instead of recording raw coordinates, which break when a room changes shape, it abstracts edits into hierarchical constraints covering local functional relationships and global topological context. A human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning component then updates retrieval policies using the final edited scene as feedback.

In a mixed-design user study with 42 participants plus an offline ablation, the authors report fewer corrective edits and lower physical demand, along with layouts that follow the user's profile rather than shallow object-level traits. The abstract gives no effect sizes, so how large the improvement is cannot be judged. The core idea, learning the logic behind a user's edits rather than their literal placements, is sound and the reduced physical strain is a believable and useful outcome in VR. With N=42 and no stated magnitudes, I regard it as a solid human-computer interaction contribution rather than a decisive one.

Nomad: generating city mobility with no local trajectories

Synthetic human mobility trajectories are useful for urban analysis, but most generators need trajectory data from the city where they will be used, which excludes just the cities lacking such data. Nomad studies a strict setting: learn from points of interest and trajectories in source cities, then use only POI coordinates and categories in the target city. No target trajectory or trajectory-derived statistic is allowed, even for model selection.

The key move is to stop predicting absolute destinations, which tangle reusable behavior with a particular city's POI identities and layout, and to predict context-conditioned relative transitions. A history-conditioned flow-matching model learns a prior over semantic displacement between POI contexts, geographic displacement and elapsed time. At generation time, a behavior graph and an exploration–return walk ground the sampled transitions onto the target city's actual POI map. In effect, how people move is learned separately from where the movement lands.

Across ten cities and 14 transfers, Nomad is reported to beat adaptation baselines, reducing average error by about 15% in distributional fidelity and about 3% in downstream utility relative to the best baseline for each metric. The 15% fidelity gain is meaningful, while the 3% utility gain is modest and may sit within what a downstream user would notice little. The strict protocol, banning target-derived statistics even for model selection, is the paper's most credible feature, because many transfer results quietly leak. The abstract does not say how the cities differ culturally or in size, which governs how far the transferred behavior can be trusted.

item.title: Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
item.summary:
AI agents can each make locally valid decisions yet jointly produce an invalid result. We call this the global coherence problem: a failure of shared state, not merely of model intelligence.
  Our Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact boundary. A policy can guarantee a valid action exactly when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action. If k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k; more reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction. A stronger model can reason better within its context, but it cannot see beyond it.
  We then give local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D): topology H records overlapping scopes; category C governs state-changing actions; groupoid G retains reversible translations; sheaf F tests whether local views glue into one world; and minimal history D keeps only distinctions that alter legal futures. Models propose; the harness owns shared state and governs commit.
  Nine studies test both the failure and its boundary. On a controlled revision benchmark, the same frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible; when it is hidden, tested arms score 12--17/40, consistent with chance (1/3); restoring one authoritative fact returns 40/40. On TeamBench, ordinary teams exceed a shared budget in 5/5 runs, a visible live count leaves 4/5 violations, and commit enforcement leaves 0/5. In tau2-bench Telecom, current-state checks score 0.07 after silent reverts, while the harness scores 1.00. Where a conventional solver already owns the complete relevant state, it ties the harness as predicted. The counterintuitive conclusion is that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state.

items.context: In multi-agent systems, agents may act on different or incomplete views of a shared situation, so individually valid decisions can conflict when combined. The abstract describes this as a shared-state and coordination problem, and proposes runtime mechanisms for checking whether local views agree before actions are committed. These are the source’s framing and proposed semantics; its specific theorem and benchmark results are claims reported in the abstract, not general background facts.
items.why: The abstract is worth reading for its precise account of when missing information limits coordination: it claims that agents cannot reliably distinguish worlds that look identical to them but require incompatible actions. It also reports tests where commit enforcement prevented budget violations and a harness handled silent reverts better than current-state checks, while matching a conventional solver when that solver had the complete relevant state. These examples make the proposed distinction between better reasoning and better shared-state management concrete.

item.title: Anatomy of a Lean proof for software engineers
item.summary: [Contents]IntroBackground: DFAs & Regular LanguagesDeterministic Finite Automaton (DFA)Regular LanguagesThe ProblemThe SolutionAdder ArithmeticAdder DFAExample 1Example 2The Lean ProofThe SpecificationThe ImplementationHow Proofs WorkThe ProofRun InvariantRun Invariant ProofBase CaseInductive StepSplitting the RunFirst Step AddsLeast Significant Bit SplitPutting It TogetherBRB^{\mathcal{R}} Is RegularAdder DFA Accepts BRB^{\mathcal{R}}From Acceptance to RegularityBB Is RegularOutroIntroI recently worked through a problem from a theory of computation textbook that asked me to prove a property of a language using finite automata. The informal proof is a simple constructive proof where you build an automaton and show that it recognizes the language. This is kind of similar to program verification, so I thought it’d be interesting to see what it takes to formalize the proof. Lean is a good choice for this, because its Mathlib has all the theorems for the problem.After finishing the formal proof, I decided to write it up, because I think it provides software engineers with good insight into what it takes to formally prove properties of a system.I tried to make this post accessible. If you’re comfortable with a modern statically typed programming language (such as TypeScript or Rust), binary arithmetic, basic propositional logic, and inductive proofs, you should be able to follow along.Background: DFAs & Regular LanguagesFeel free to skip to the next section if you’re comfortable with DFAs and regular languages.Finite automata provide a theoretical model of computation with fixed memory. Besides theory, finite automata also have important practical applications. For example, finite automata are relevant for parsers and regular expressions, where a bug once took a significant portion of the internet down.Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA)A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a machine with a fixed, finite set of states that reads its input one symbol at a time, left to right. With each symbol, it updates its state using a deterministic transition function. After the last symbol, the machine either sits in an accepting state (input is accepted) or not (input is rejected).If you’ve ever written a simple regular expression like -?[0-9]+, then you’ve constructed a DFA. This regex matches integer literals like 12 and -123 and the corresponding DFA looks like this (the arrows are annotated with the symbols that lead to the next state):DFA for a decimal integer literal, including the dead statestartsigndigitsdead-0-90-90-9otherotherotheranyThis DFA has four states:Start: this is where we start before processing the first character. Since the start state is not an accepting state, we reject the empty string.Sign: we move to the sign state when we encounter the - character in the start state. We can skip the sign state and jump directly to digits from start, since the sign character is optional (-?). If we’re in this state at the end of the string, then we reject the string.Digits: we move from start or sign to digits when we encounter a digit character ([0-9]). If we’re in the digits state and encounter a digit character again, then we stay in the digits state. The digits state is the only accepting state of the DFA. If we’re in this state after we’ve processed the input string, then the DFA accepts the string.Dead: we get into this state if we encounter any other character than a digit (unless it’s a negative sign at the start). If we’re in the dead state at the end of the string, then the DFA rejects the string. items.context: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) reads symbols one at a time, updates among finitely many states, and accepts or rejects at the end; a language is regular when some DFA accepts exactly its strings. The source applies these ideas to strings of three-bit columns encoding two addends and their sum. Since addition is easiest from least significant bit to most significant, it considers the reversed language, then uses the general closure of regular languages under reversal. These are background concepts; the source’s particular contribution is to formalize this construction and its proof in Lean.
items.why: The article offers a worked example of turning an informal, constructive automata argument into a Lean proof, with sections on the specification, implementation, and a run invariant proved by base case and inductive step. Its focus on a concrete arithmetic example may help software engineers see how formal proofs connect a system’s behavior to a stated property.

item.title: Mimir: Physics-Grounded LLM Agents for Long-Horizon Irrigation Control
item.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly combine reasoning, tool use, and action, but most evidence comes from episodic tasks with relatively immediate feedback and reset failures. Long-running physical control operates in a different regime: actions alter future states, errors compound across decisions, and an agent must improve from experience without being allowed to rewrite the physical rules that make execution safe. We study this regime through irrigation, where daily decisions interact with soil-water dynamics over entire growing seasons. We present Mimir, a physics-grounded LLM agent organized around two repair timescales. At the fast timescale, a structured physical interface and deterministic simulator turn an LLM output into a proposal that we numerically check, revise, and subject to bounded deterministic action selection before execution. At the slow timescale, recurrent failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles that condition future proposals, while the physical model, evaluator, and execution constraints remain immutable. Under a common retrospective evaluator across multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir attains the lowest reported aggregate control cost among the evaluated references and uses about 51% less irrigation than the historical schedule replay. The ablation study show higher control cost when forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context is removed; model-scale and model-family studies show no monotonic gain from increasing LLM size. The resulting lesson show that persistent physical agents can combine semantic reasoning with bounded, evidence-driven self-improvement while reserving physical truth and actuator authority for explicit numerical mechanisms.

items.context: Long-horizon physical control differs from one-off tasks because actions change future system states and mistakes can accumulate. In irrigation, daily choices interact with soil-water dynamics over a growing season. The abstract describes an agent whose language-model proposals are checked and bounded by a numerical simulator; these are the source’s design choices, not general requirements for every control system.
items.why: The abstract reports lower aggregate control cost than the evaluated references and about 51% less irrigation than replaying historical schedules, under a shared retrospective evaluator across sites, crops, and years. Its ablations also report higher costs when key components are removed, making the work relevant to readers interested in how simulation, verification, and persistent learning might support safer long-running agents.

items.context: Text-to-image systems create images from written prompts, while image-editing systems modify selected parts of an existing image. Bounding boxes can specify where elements should appear or which regions to edit, and reference images can guide a generated composition. This post presents FLUX 3 Image as supporting these workflows, including high-resolution output; those are claims in the supplied extract, not independently verified findings.
items.why: The extract is useful as a snapshot of the image-generation and editing workflows FLUX 3 Image promotes: prompt-based creation, box-guided layout, multiple references, targeted edits, and 2K/4K rendering. It may help readers assess the tool’s stated capabilities, though the partial post does not provide independent performance evidence.

item.title: CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.summary: Recent years have witnessed the rapid adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) in large language model (LLM) post-training, with substantial gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation. In practical systems, however, policy updates and differences between rollout and training engines can make sampled responses off-policy. Sequence-level masking addresses this mismatch by deciding whether an entire response should contribute to optimization. A common masking rule uses the length-normalized geometric mean of sampled token probability ratios. Its signed log-ratios can cancel across positions, concealing substantial bidirectional policy drift. We propose \emph{Cancellation-Aware Response Masking} (CARM), a sequence-level mask that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging, preventing opposing probability changes from canceling. We prove that accepted responses satisfy a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios outside a prescribed band and their mean log-distance beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that CARM improves mean@16 averaged over AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME by up to $3.13$ percentage points over geometric-mean masking, and increases average pass@1 across four code benchmarks by $2.88$ points over the strongest evaluated baseline. These findings support CARM as a theoretically grounded and effective method for response-level off-policy control in LLM reinforcement learning.

items.context: In LLM reinforcement learning, a model is updated using sampled responses, but differences between the system that generates those responses and the one used for training can make them off-policy. Sequence-level masking decides whether a whole response contributes to an update. The abstract says a common rule averages token probability ratios geometrically; CARM instead averages the absolute token log-ratios so opposing changes cannot cancel. These are the source’s method description and claims, rather than general background facts about all RL systems.
items.why: The abstract presents both a theoretical result—a joint bound on token-ratio deviations for accepted responses—and benchmark results: improvements over geometric-mean masking on mathematical reasoning and over the strongest evaluated baseline on code generation. It may be useful to readers interested in how response-level masking can address policy drift in LLM reinforcement learning; these results are reported in the abstract, not independently assessed here.

item.title: Loss of cell identity drives human aging: Two new papers
item.summary: Two new papers, one published today in Nature by Vadim Gladyshev and colleagues at Harvard, and a recent one in Cell by Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte and his team at Altos Labs, have provided a new model for the biology of aging, and what might be done to reverse it. Until recently we accepted that aging of cells was due to “wear and tear” like rusting out a car. The idea that accumulated damage is the principal pathway for cell aging is now complemented by the loss of cell identity model. We don’t know the relative contribution or interdependence of these 2 models in the aging process. Two different models for why cells age, made with ChatGPT In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to explain the loss of cell identity, how it leads to mesenchymal drift (fibrous scarring and inflammation), and how this new model furthers the potential to intervene in the aging process. Share Ground TruthsIn embryonic and early development, our cells establish an identity. It’s locked in throughout our lives, except when it’s lost during the aging process. Although the DNA of every cell of our body is the same (or very close, if interested, see), the epigenetic structure, that includes methylation side chains, histones, nucleosomes and chromatin, is 3-dimensional and differs as a function of cell type. This is happening in the cell’s “mission control,” the nucleus. The epigenetic structure is the bedrock for our cell-specific identity.There’s a 3-tier regulatory “grammar” that maintains the cell identity as shown below.(Figure from the Nature paper). The fast layer responds to acute stress in a matter of minutes to hours and relies on production of transcription factors, like AP-1. The intermediate layer takes days to weeks to respond, going through cell state transitions such as activating a cell to promote healing and return to its basal state. The key is the slow layer, he one that locks and insulates the cell identity, the hard boundary, relying on chromatin architecture.That gets us to Waddington’s epigenetic landscape model for how cells differentiate or de-differentiate, a model that has held up well from Conrad Waddington in 1957! A cell sitting down in the valley (Figure below, culled together from the Nature paper) represents a distinct specialized cell. The deep slope indicates the robustness, also called canalization, accompanied by a deep basin, maintains the identity of the cell, promotes its stability. The differentiated cell is “staying in its lane” in the landscape model and is constrained from sliding out, shifting identity. But with aging, the valleys lose their slope, the basin becomes shallow, there is loss of epigenetic constraints, and there is instability of cell identity. That sets up drift of cell identity, or what can be regarded as mesenchymal drift.Over the lifespan, as shown on the right side of the Figure below, after peak maturation with the specialized cells (brain, liver heart,kidney, etc) fully and irrevocably differentiated (peak functional state below), the valleys are losing slope and the basins are progressively getting shallower, known as decanalization. The problem is that there is no evolutionary pressure to keep the grooves, valleys and basin in their youthful state, because the “selection shadow” is a post-reproductive trajectory.The polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) can be seen as the sculptor of this epigenetic landscape, the molecular machinery that shapes the grooves, valleys, and basin. It establishes the hard boundary, the deep epigenetic constraints for cell identity.Epigenetic clocks are remarkably informative across 348 mammalian species, including humans, for predicting maximal lifespan and life history, but we didn’t know what they are actually measuring. It turns out it’s PRC2, the pace of slow layer erosion! (Figure below, to be precise, it’s the PRC2 low-methylated regions).PRC2 comes into play when there is chronic inflammation overriding the fast layer capacity to respond and blocking PRC2, leading to erosion of the Waddington landscape, promoting cell identity loss. Even after chronic inflammation is resolved, there are epigenetic changes in chromatin that can persist. This loss of epigenetic grammar can also be the foundation for cancer cells. Eventual erosion of the slow layer essentially portends architectural collapse of the Waddington landscape.Schematic of PRC2, what epigenetic clocks are capturing. Made with Google NotebookThe mesenchymal state, as schematically shown below, in this example for an epithelial cell representative of all differentiated, specialized cells. Schematic of drift, made with Google NotebookNow we turn to the Cell paper which goes deep on the mesenchymal drift. This denotes the change of cells to a mesenchymal state, resembling fibroblasts, engendering fibrous scar, laying down extracellular matrix, like mushy putty. It has been verified in 46 tissue types and is part and parcel of disease progression and poor outcomes, as shown below (Figure from the Cell paper). If you are checking for the tie-in between mesenchymal drift and age-related diseases, you’ll find them here, from atherosclerosis, to age-related macular degeneration, to Alzheimer’s disease. Now that we have an enhanced understanding of the process, which has a positive feedback loop as depicted below, fibroblast sthat are activating in turn activating more fibroblasts to induce scarring (Figure from the Cell paper), how can we intervene to freeze the drift, avoid the slow layer erosion, and preserve the Waddington landscape, keeping cells locked in their designated identity? Or, even more ambitious, actually turn back the loss of erosion that has occurred?Caloric restriction (CR), with its attendant reduced acetyl CoA, and reduced PRC2 methylation, promotes the preservation of slow layer architecture, conceptually freezing the drift. CR has been shown to promote lifespan in mammalian species but the results in non-human primates have been inconsistent, and the magnitude and duration of caloric restriction likely required in people is impractical. Still there may be, theoretically, a partial effect of avoidance of high caloric intake to help prevent erosion.The use of the Yamanaka stem cell factors is the far-reaching intervention—rejuvenating cells— that has attracted the most attention and huge investment by biotech companies. But it’s tricky because it requires a brief exposure to the 4 transcription factors, OSKM (Oct-4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), called “partial” epigenetic reprogramming, in order to avoid full reprogramming, which erases their memory and turns cells into pluripotent stem cells. That carries an increased risk for cancer. But partial reprogramming using short bursts, rejuvenation is seen, with restoration of cell identity in aged human fibroblasts (even from age 96 years) and in animal models. The slow layer is restored, the PRC2 domains are re-established, and the mesenchymal drift is actively reversed. An alternative to short exposure for partial reprogramming is the use of 3 transcription factors OSK (no c-Myc) which is being tested in a pilot study of patients with severe optic nerve damage using direct eye injection.The Nature paper also gets into lithium as an intervention for maintaining neuron identity by interfering with the pathway of slow layer failure. I won’t get into the details of all the mediators (β-catenin, EDH2-USP7, KDM1A, REST, GSK3β, etc) but lithium’s impact on GSK3β blocks tau phosphorylation in experimental models. Lithium orotate has been raised as a candidate for preventing Alzheimer’s, as I’ve previously written about, and this mechanism may be operative. There continues to be extraordinary progress in the science of aging. Beyond the old dogma that this is just the cumulative outgrowth of cell mutations and damage, we now understand the epigenetic basis: the loss of cell identity serves as both a driver and result of the aging process. items.context: Cell identity is the specialized state of a cell, maintained in part by epigenetic regulation of how DNA is organized and used; Waddington’s landscape is a metaphor for how stable or changeable cell states can be. The source presents loss of this stability as a model that complements the familiar idea of aging through accumulated cellular damage. It reports that the papers it discusses link age-related epigenetic changes with drift toward mesenchymal, scar-forming cell states, while noting that the models’ relative contributions remain unknown.
items.why: The material offers a readable synthesis of two recent papers, connecting proposed mechanisms of cell aging to tissue scarring and possible interventions such as partial epigenetic reprogramming. It also distinguishes promising experimental results from unresolved questions, including the risks of reprogramming and the uncertain relevance of some approaches to people.

item.title: SPHERE: Adaptive VR Indoor Scene Generation via LLM-Enhanced Spatial Preference Learning and Human-in-the-Loop RL
item.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance 3D indoor scene synthesis, current pipelines fail to retain user-specific preferences across sessions, making immersive authoring a repetitive and physically fatiguing process. We present SPHERE, an adaptive VR generation framework that transforms isolated synthesis into continuous human-AI co-creation. SPHERE extracts persistent spatial preferences from natural multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits). To ensure geometric resilience against spatial distortions, it abstracts these raw edits into hierarchical constraints modeling both local functional and global topological contexts. Furthermore, a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning mechanism dynamically updates retrieval policies based on the user's final edited scenes. A mixed-design user study ($N=42$) and an offline ablation demonstrate that SPHERE significantly reduces corrective edits and physical demand, preventing bias toward shallow object-level traits to yield geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. Ultimately, SPHERE demonstrates how capturing demonstrated spatial logic enables controlled spatial adaptation, establishing a reliable, governed human-AI collaboration framework for immersive authoring. Project page and source code will be available at: https://github.com/hyeonmin11/SPHERE

items.context: VR indoor scene generation uses software to create room layouts for immersive environments. In general, language models can help synthesize scenes, while speech and controller edits provide ways for users to express preferences. The abstract describes SPHERE as carrying preferences across sessions by representing edits as hierarchical constraints—covering local functional and global topological relationships—and updating retrieval policies through human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning. These are the paper’s proposed methods, not general guarantees about such systems.
items.why: The abstract may interest readers exploring adaptive creative tools and human-AI collaboration: it reports a mixed-design study with 42 participants and an offline ablation, claiming fewer corrective edits and reduced physical demand, while retaining geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. These are claims from the abstract; assessing their evidence and limitations would require the full paper.

item.title: Relative Transitions, Not Absolute Destinations: A Transfer-and-Ground Framework for Target-Trajectory-Free Human Mobility Generation
item.summary: Individual mobility trajectories support urban analysis and location-based services, yet most trajectory generators require observations from their deployment city. This assumption excludes precisely the cities where trajectories are unavailable even though points of interest (POIs) and their attributes can be obtained from public maps. We study target-trajectory-free generation: learning from POIs and trajectories in source cities while utilizing only POI coordinates and categories in a target city, with no target trajectory or trajectory-derived statistic available for training, model selection, or generation. Existing trajectory generators typically predict absolute destinations, entangling reusable movement behavior with city-specific POI identities and spatial layouts. Our core insight is to replace this city-bound output with context-conditioned relative transitions. We propose Nomad, a transfer-and-ground framework that separates learning how people move from determining where those movements are realized. Specifically, a history-conditioned flow-matching model learns from source trajectories a transition prior over semantic displacement between POI contexts, geographic displacement, and elapsed time; at inference, a behavior graph and an exploration--return walk ground sampled transitions onto the target POI map. This factorization enables a direct test of representation level transferability without assuming invariance of the full mobility distribution. Extensive experiments across ten cities and 14 transfers show that Nomad outperforms adaptation baselines in trajectory fidelity and downstream utility, lowering the average error over the best baseline of each metric by about 15% in distributional fidelity and about 3% in downstream utility.

items.context: Points of interest (POIs) are mapped locations with attributes such as categories. Mobility trajectories record sequences of visits and movements. This abstract describes a setting where a model learns movement patterns from source cities but has access only to POI coordinates and categories—not trajectories or trajectory-derived statistics—in a target city. It contrasts predicting absolute destinations with modeling relative transitions conditioned on POI context, geographic displacement, and elapsed time; these are concepts in the proposed approach, not established guarantees of transferability.
items.why: The abstract is useful for readers interested in generating mobility trajectories when target-city trajectory data is unavailable. It outlines Nomad’s separation of learned movement behavior from mapping that behavior onto a target city’s POIs, and reports tests across ten cities and 14 transfers. The authors report better trajectory fidelity than adaptation baselines and improvements in downstream utility, while the abstract alone does not provide the full experimental details.
